v1-tdd-escape.title: TDD not_yet_written escape hatch closed?
v1-tdd-escape.imperative: Reproduce the Admiral's single-condition not_yet_written gate refusal (falsifiable-all-null). Then attack: try to build ANY spec (multi-gate, mixed kinds, qualitative paired with it) that uses not_yet_written to reach a WRITTEN spine with no check that can ever fail. BLOCK if found.
v1-tdd-escape.finding: PASS -- not_yet_written cannot reach a written GATED spine with an unfalsifiable gate. Reproduced the Admiral's repro first: a single not_yet_written pytest postcondition -> exit 4, [falsifiable-all-null]. Then built 5 adversarial specs myself (not reusing the crew's or Admiral's fixtures): (A) single-condition -- refused. (B) not_yet_written + qualitative in one gate (both null) -- refused, all-null still fires since it checks the COMPILED check value, not the spec-level kind. (C) two not_yet_written pytest conditions in one gate -- refused. (D) multi-gate spread: one real gate (population check) + one all-null gate -- the WHOLE spine refuses to write (exit 4, no file emitted), confirmed a fault anywhere blocks the entire generation, not just that gate. (E) SURVEY-type spec with a lone not_yet_written postcondition -- this one DOES generate clean (exit 0), because validate_spine._fault_all_null explicitly returns [] for spine_type != GATED. Investigated whether this is a new hole: it is not -- read checklist_engine.record()'s own code and its #422 D-scope ruling comment: record() evaluates command-kind postconditions only; null-kind and artifact-kind postconditions on ANY survey item (with or without not_yet_written) are explicitly, already unevaluated by design -- the same treatment every qualitative postcondition on every existing survey template already receives. not_yet_written on a survey item is therefore not a new escape, it is one more instance of an already-known, already-floated architecture gap (record/consolidate never evaluate null/artifact postconditions on a survey item -- tc1 in g2-review's own triage_candidates). Also independently found and separately verified: the earlier spec-shape-time informational check spec-all-qualitative-postconditions does NOT recognize a not_yet_written pytest condition (its kind stays 'pytest', not 'qualitative'), so it does not warn early on an all-not_yet_written gate -- but this is redundant, cosmetic-only: the unconditional downstream oracle (validate_spine.validate(), the literal last statement before success) still catches every case tried. No BLOCK.

v3-truthiness-bug.title: not_yet_written bare-truthiness misread — judge the call
v3-truthiness-bug.imperative: cond.get('not_yet_written') is read with bare truthiness, so a string 'false' is truthy and misread as a declaration. The crew named this and left it as out-of-scope. Judge: is shipping this known misreading acceptable, or a BLOCK?
v3-truthiness-bug.finding: JUDGMENT: acceptable to ship, not a BLOCK, but a real defect that should be fixed next round -- not silently closed. Reproduced directly: compile_condition({...,'not_yet_written':'false'}) compiles to check:None and the NOT-YET-WRITTEN statement text, and _cond_faults raises zero faults for it -- confirmed the misread is real, not hypothetical. Reasoning for non-BLOCK: (1) it is an authoring footgun, not a hostile-author escape -- an author who WANTS to weaken a check can already do so legitimately with not_yet_written=true; this bug only bites an author who did NOT intend to weaken the check and mistyped a truthy string. (2) it never lets a gate reach 'no check that can ever fail' as a WHOLE (that is v1's bar, and v1 held under every attack I built) -- in a single-condition gate the mistake still surfaces as a hard refusal (falsifiable-all-null) because the resulting check is still null; in a multi-condition gate it silently disables machine verification of just that one condition while the gate as a whole still has a real check, which is a real but narrower harm than v1's concern. (3) it was self-reported with precise reasoning in IMPLEMENTER_RESULT.md, not discovered by me first or hidden. (4) the fix is small and mechanical (an isinstance(value, bool)-style guard, matching Blocker 1's own pattern) but was not in Blocker 1's named 4-field scope, so treating its absence as a blocker this round would be scope-creep against the handoff's own boundary. Recommend: promote to a concrete next-round item (not just left as a mention), since it is a value-correctness bug hiding behind a working mechanism -- exactly the class this review's own doctrine warns about.
